$comment: Minimum number of tests each suite must actually run, asserted by
tools/check-test-count.mjs. A green exit code is not evidence that a
suite ran. Measured on Node 24.21: `node --test test/` runs 0 real
tests and exits 1, but `node --test 'test/*.nope.ts'` runs 0 tests and
exits 0. One typo in a glob turns a whole suite into a silent green.
Raise a number here when you add tests. Do not lower one to make CI
green: a drop normally means tests stopped being discovered or stopped
existing, and both are the failure this gate is for.
## The one legitimate decrease: retiring a ledger test
packages/alc/test/known-defects.test.ts pins each open defect from the
adversarial pass (docs/alc-1-attack-report.md) with a test asserting
that the defect STILL REPRODUCES. Those tests are green while the
defect is open and go red when it is fixed, and the failure message is
the instruction: replace the characterisation test with the real
assertion it was standing in for. Defects pinned in the suite that will
own the guarantee behave the same way.
So a fix can legitimately lower this suite's count. One guarantee often
replaces several characterisation tests, and the matching KNOWN_DEFECTS
entry in packages/alc/test/fuzz/invariants.ts goes away with it. That
case was not written down here, which left the only sanctioned
decrease looking exactly like the failure above.
It is still not self-certified. To lower minTests:
1. Follow the protocol in the failing test's message and in the
known-defects.test.ts header in full. Re-measure with the
measurement that found the defect — not with the assertion
flipping. Replace the characterisation test with the guarantee,
under a title that does NOT carry the QA-<n> id. Delete the
KNOWN_DEFECTS entry. Flip the report row to `**fixed** in <sha>`
and fix the counts sentence under the table. Skip a step and the
suite goes red naming the step you skipped.
2. Re-measure the whole suite and set minTests to the count actually
observed on the committed tree. Never to a round number, never to
an estimate, and never below what ran.
3. Add a `retirements` entry below: the defect id, the commit that
fixed it, and the count before and after. An undocumented drop in
this file's history reads exactly like the bug this gate catches;
the entry is what makes the drop reviewable instead.
Any decrease that is not a ledger retirement under that protocol: find
the tests.

The DOG-37 research layer: the schema validator, both browse modes, the solid-colour layer computation, the trust boundary, and the curated seed set. Per-file counts on the committed tree, so a drop can be localised without bisecting: schema 33, browse 20, layers 28, trust 16, seed 18, citations 9 = 124. Raised 113 -> 124 on DOG-46, which is a correction as much as an addition: DOG-50 added citations.test.ts without moving the floor, so nine tests were running unprotected and deleting that whole file would have left this gate green. Two of the eleven are DOG-46's own, both in schema.test.ts: a partitioned dataset must say per structure which index should name it, and structureIdSources must describe the namespaces the mappings actually use. Three of those files carry a must-pass case, and the floor is only meaningful while they do. browse.test.ts has `the leak detector would catch a leak`, which builds a selection deliberately intersected with the anatomical filter and asserts the comparison used by the filter-leak test can see the difference — without it, that test would pass against an implementation that leaked. seed.test.ts has `the resolution check can fail`, which points a mapping at a structure id the index does not have and asserts it surfaces as `unknown-structure` painting nothing. layers.test.ts pins the palette's exact hexes and slot order, because the order is the colour-vision safety mechanism and re-ordering it is a measurement rather than a preference. Deleting any of those three lowers the count and removes the evidence that the gate above it can go red.
